sources.title: async-utils: Support BandwidthPool partial permit
passages:
The first commit removes the rate limited `Sink` object as it is not used anywhere and there are no plans for now to use it. Reason is that partial permits complicate quite a bit that sink implementation.

Only the fast path can emit partial commit and with a minimum grant value (floor). Reason only the fast path emits them is because we want to avoid the "ping pong" effect I _**cleverly**_ named.

For example, 1 token in the pool, a claim for 10 arrives, we give out 1. Then the caller can't use that 1 token so refunds it and comes back with a claim of 10. I think one can see where this will go... To mitigate that, we make the slow path wait for the entirety of the request so we avoid this problem and also avoid the problem of deciding what is the minimum wait time we will use to start emitting partial permits.

For the floor, it is so we avoid connections being given the refunds breadcrumbs of very few tokens and waste CPU time with syscall(s) for very few bytes. So, for our channels, we can set that `min_grant` to the size of a cell so any partial permit will at the very least allow to read or write a full cell.

Ticket #2834

sources.title: relay: Handle drain rate updates in the stream reactor
passages:
Send a drain rate update through the forward reactor to the stream
reactor which checks the stream's XON/XOFF state. It can then decide to

backward reactor.

This problem came out after arti-relay Chutney testing for which the

crash the relay.

During testing, the arti-relay would send an XOFF but then never an XON

I suspect that this issue is actually related to https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/41420. Under the CBT timeout calculation problems in that bug, Tor will keep creating new channels to the guard, making both situations much worse.

I am preparing a fix on top of that MR.

passages:
Our fix for #41360, #41365, and #41366 prevents remotely-induced Guard rotation cases.

However, we did not change the code in `circuit_build_failed()` that marks `is_bad_for_new_circs = 1` for the channel.

This means that an adversary can still use these triggers (and the other ones David found while working on https://gitlab.torproject.org/dgoulet/tor-private/-/merge_requests/33) to cause clients to create an additional TLS connection to their existing Guard. 

This effect can be observed by [netflow adversaries](https://spec.torproject.org/proposals/344-protocol-info-leaks.html#131-netflow-observation), potentially allowing them to confirm that a particular client was taking a particular action.

This is much much less severe than inducing Guard rotation, since the outcome is not immediate or definite. Existing circuits will continue to use the "bad for new circuits" TLS connection. New circuits might use the other guard before creating a new TLS connection.

Still, this is not a great property. If we can fix it simply, we should.. However it might not be simple to fix without some additional mechanism to ensure we actually *do* give up on channels that are dead due to transient network conditions.

We should at least have an LLM enumerate as many of these cases as possible for us, so we can weigh if any of them would be useful for an adversary (such as one that wants to make an onion service use a new TLS connection, or one that wants to make a client use a new TLS connection once it has been observed to be doing some specific activity).

Cc: @dgoulet

passages.text:
@roypranto39 - it sounds like one of your guards could be experiencing a DoS attack? There is also a possibility that your services themselves are being connected to by clients specifying broken or slow rendezvous points (this could be an attack, but more likely is a consequence of network DoS conditions elsewhere).

In either case, setting the following torrc should change the behavior and at least prevent the issue from causing connectivity problems:

```code
LearnCircuitBuildTimeout 0
CircuitBuildTimeout 60
```

It would be useful to know if this does in fact address the connectivity issue for your services. If it solves the connectivity problem, it will rule out other potential causes.

Note that this will degrade performance of your service, so once we have a fix you should remove these lines.

sources.title: prop327: Implement PoW over Introduction Circuits
passages: This is an initial implementation of new functionality for mitigating DoS attacks on onion services using a proof-of-work client puzzle
This addresses ticket #40634 and provides an initial implementation.
As noted in the ticket there's room for improvement, but at this stage the feature might be considered useful and the wire protocol stabilized.
To get the new proof-of-work system, clients and services must both be built with `--enable-gpl` and services must have the `HiddenServicePoWDefensesEnabled` torrc option at runtime.

sources.title: Changes in version 0.4.8.4 - 2023-08-23
passages: Finally, this is the very first stable release of the 0.4.8.x series making, among other features, Proof-of-Work (prop#327) and Conflux (prop#329) available to the entire network.
Implement Proposal 329 (conflux traffic splitting). Conflux splits traffic across two circuits to Exits that support the protocol.
When using conflux circuit pairs, clients choose the lower-latency circuit to send data to the Exit.
When the Exit sends data to the client, it maximizes throughput, by fully utilizing both circuits in a multiplexed fashion.
Onion services are not currently supported, but will be in arti.

sources.title: Counter Galois Onion: Improved encryption for Tor circuit traffic
passages: Especially when we are sunsetting one of the oldest and most important encryption algorithms in Tor and replacing it with a research-backed new design, called Counter Galois Onion.
This overhaul will defend users against a broader class of online attackers (described below), and form the basis for more encryption work in the future.
CGO makes it so that if anybody tampers with any part of your encrypted data, the entire message, and all future messages, become unrecoverable.
We've also implemented it in C, since it won't do us any good unless relays support it too, and the Arti relay project is still a work in progress.

sources.title: Changes in version 0.4.9.5 - 2026-02-12
passages: This first stable release in the 0.4.9 series introduces a new circuit-level encryption design for better client security, as well as a more scalable way for large relay operators to annotate which relays they run so clients can avoid using too many of them in a single circuit.
Clients and relays now support "happy families", a system to simplify relay family operation and improve directory performance.
With "happy families", relays in a family share a secret "family key", which they use to prove their membership in the family.
Note that until enough clients are upgraded, relay operators will still need to configure MyFamily lists.
But once clients no longer depend on those lists, we will be able to remove them entirely, thereby simplifying family operation, and making microdescriptor downloads approximately 80% smaller.

Now we're announcing the latest release, Arti 1.3.0.

Now we're announcing the latest release, Arti 1.4.2.

sources.title: Arti 1.1.6 is released: Now you can connect* to Onion Services!
passages: After months of hard work, Arti finally has working client-side onion service support!
That is, programs can* now use Arti to connect to onion services on the Tor network.
Note that this feature is not yet as secure as the equivalent feature in the C tor implementation, and as such you probably shouldn't use it for security-sensitive purposes.
For this reason, the feature is (for now) disabled by default.

sources.title: Hiding in plain sight: Introducing WebTunnel
passages: Today, March 12th, on the World Day Against Cyber Censorship, the Tor Project's Anti-Censorship Team is excited to officially announce the release of WebTunnel, a new type of Tor bridge designed to assist users in heavily censored regions to connect to the Tor network.
Available now in the stable version of Tor Browser, WebTunnel joined our collection of censorship circumvention tech developed and maintained by The Tor Project.
WebTunnel is a censorship-resistant pluggable transport designed to mimic encrypted web traffic (HTTPS) inspired by HTTPT.
It works by wrapping the payload connection into a WebSocket-like HTTPS connection, appearing to network observers as an ordinary HTTPS (WebSocket) connection.
WebTunnel can be used as an alternative to obfs4 for most Tor Browser users.

sources.title: New Release: Tor Browser 14.5
passages: This release marks the introduction of Connection Assist to Android, empowering mobile users who are subjected to strict censorship to unblock Tor at the press of a button.
Subsequently, should Tor Browser fail to establish a direct connection to the Tor network, Connection Assist will offer to find and try bridges for you.
This project has now reached an important milestone, and we're proud to announce the release of Connection Assist for Android today.
On a human level, not only is Connection Assist now available for Android, but Tor Browser users can expect more stable and less error-prone connections in general.

sources.title: New Release: Tor Browser 15.0
passages: This is our first stable release based on Firefox ESR 140, incorporating a year's worth of changes that have been shipped upstream in Firefox.
For desktop, these include vertical tabs: providing a more manageable, alternative layout with open and pinned tabs stacked in a sidebar rather than across the top of the window.

However, regardless of whether you prefer horizontal or vertical tabs, everyone benefits from the addition of tab groups: helping you keep on top of the clutter by organizing tabs into collapsible groups that can be given names and color-coded.
On Android, screen lock adds an extra layer of security to your browsing sessions.
After enabling screen lock in Settings > Tabs, your tabs will lock automatically when you switch away from the browser without closing it.

sources.title: New Release: Tor Browser 16.0
passages: This is our first stable release based on Firefox ESR 153, incorporating a year's worth of changes that have been shipped upstream in Firefox.
To that end, Tor Browser 16.0 introduces a complete redesign of the Settings experience based on a parallel redesign shipped in Firefox in June.

Pages and components that are unique to Tor browser like Connection and Security Level have been rebuilt from scratch using Firefox's new components so they look and feel consistent with the rest of Settings.
Finally, after a year of testing, Tor Browser 16.0 now features native support for Linux computers with 64-bit ARM (AArch64) processors, such as Raspberry Pis and Apple Silicon Macs running Linux.

candidate.title: Tor merges initial proof-of-work DoS mitigation for onion services
candidate.summary: A merged change to Tor adds an initial implementation of new functionality for mitigating DoS attacks on onion services using a proof-of-work client puzzle. The merge request says there is room for improvement, but at this stage the feature might be considered useful and the wire protocol stabilized. According to the merge request, to get the new proof-of-work system, clients and services must both be built with --enable-gpl, and services must have the HiddenServicePoWDefensesEnabled torrc option at runtime.

candidate.title: Tor 0.4.8.4, the first 0.4.8.x stable release, brings Conflux traffic splitting
candidate.summary: The release notes for Tor 0.4.8.4, dated 2023-08-23, call it the very first stable release of the 0.4.8.x series, making, among other features, Proof-of-Work (prop#327) and Conflux (prop#329) available to the entire network. The release implements Proposal 329 (conflux traffic splitting): Conflux splits traffic across two circuits to Exits that support the protocol. According to the notes, clients using conflux circuit pairs choose the lower-latency circuit to send data to the Exit, and the Exit maximizes throughput when sending data to the client by fully utilizing both circuits in a multiplexed fashion. The notes say onion services are not currently supported, but will be in arti.

candidate.title: Tor is replacing one of its oldest encryption algorithms with Counter Galois Onion
candidate.summary: A Tor Project blog post says Tor is sunsetting one of its oldest and most important encryption algorithms and replacing it with a research-backed new design called Counter Galois Onion (CGO), described as improved encryption for Tor circuit traffic. According to the post, CGO makes it so that if anybody tampers with any part of the encrypted data, the entire message and all future messages become unrecoverable, and the overhaul will defend users against a broader class of online attackers and form the basis for more encryption work in the future. The post says CGO has also been implemented in C, since it will not do any good unless relays support it too and the Arti relay project is still a work in progress.

candidate.title: Tor 0.4.9.5, the first 0.4.9.x stable release, introduces "happy families"
candidate.summary: The release notes for Tor 0.4.9.5, dated 2026-02-12, say this first stable release in the 0.4.9 series introduces a new circuit-level encryption design for better client security, as well as a more scalable way for large relay operators to annotate which relays they run so clients can avoid using too many of them in a single circuit. Clients and relays now support "happy families", a system to simplify relay family operation and improve directory performance, in which relays in a family share a secret "family key" that they use to prove their membership in the family. The notes say relay operators will still need to configure MyFamily lists until enough clients are upgraded; once clients no longer depend on those lists, the lists can be removed entirely, which the notes say will simplify family operation and make microdescriptor downloads approximately 80% smaller.

candidate.summary: Arti 1.1.6 has been released, and its announcement says Arti now has working client-side onion service support: programs can now use Arti to connect to onion services on the Tor network. The announcement notes that the feature is not yet as secure as the equivalent feature in the C tor implementation, and probably should not be used for security-sensitive purposes; for this reason, it is (for now) disabled by default.

candidate.title: Tor Project releases WebTunnel, a new bridge type for users in heavily censored regions
candidate.summary: On March 12th, the World Day Against Cyber Censorship, the Tor Project's Anti-Censorship Team officially announced the release of WebTunnel, a new type of Tor bridge designed to assist users in heavily censored regions to connect to the Tor network. WebTunnel is available in the stable version of Tor Browser. It is a censorship-resistant pluggable transport, inspired by HTTPT, designed to mimic encrypted web traffic (HTTPS): it wraps the payload connection into a WebSocket-like HTTPS connection, appearing to network observers as an ordinary HTTPS (WebSocket) connection. The announcement says WebTunnel can be used as an alternative to obfs4 for most Tor Browser users.

The announcement describes Connection Assist as offering to find and try bridges should Tor Browser fail to establish a direct connection to the Tor network.

candidate.title: Tor Browser 15.0 released with vertical tabs, tab groups and Android screen lock

According to the announcement, for desktop these include vertical tabs, an alternative layout with open and pinned tabs stacked in a sidebar rather than across the top of the window. The announcement also highlights the addition of tab groups, which organize tabs into collapsible groups that can be given names and color-coded. On Android, the announcement says screen lock adds an extra layer of security to browsing sessions: after it is enabled in Settings > Tabs, tabs lock automatically when the user switches away from the browser without closing it.

candidate.title: Tor Browser 16.0 released with redesigned Settings and native 64-bit ARM Linux support
candidate.summary: Tor Browser 16.0 is the first stable release based on Firefox ESR 153, incorporating a year's worth of changes that have been shipped upstream in Firefox. It introduces a complete redesign of the Settings experience based on a parallel redesign shipped in Firefox in June; pages and components unique to Tor Browser, like Connection and Security Level, have been rebuilt from scratch using Firefox's new components so they look and feel consistent with the rest of Settings. After a year of testing, Tor Browser 16.0 also features native support for Linux computers with 64-bit ARM (AArch64) processors, such as Raspberry Pis and Apple Silicon Macs running Linux.
